learn.hook: Imagine firing tiny bullets at a sheet of tissue paper and a few of them bounce straight back at you! That shocking result revealed the nucleus.
points: Dalton (1808) imagined atoms as tiny indivisible balls. J.J. Thomson's discovery of the electron (1897) showed that atoms have smaller parts inside.
Thomson's model (1904): an atom is a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it, like seeds in a watermelon. The atom as a whole is neutral.
Rutherford's gold foil experiment: fast alpha particles were fired at a very thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, some were deflected and very few bounced back.

Rutherford's model (1911): the atom is mostly empty space, with a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre and electrons revolving around it. But revolving electrons should lose energy and fall into the nucleus, so this model could not explain why atoms are stable.
Bohr's model (1913): electrons revolve only in certain special orbits, or shells (K, L, M, N...), and do not radiate energy while in these orbits.

example.q: Think it through: In Rutherford's experiment, why did very few alpha particles bounce back?
steps: Alpha particles are positively charged and fast.
To bounce back, they must hit something positive, heavy and concentrated head-on.
Since only a very few bounced back, this positive, heavy part must be tiny.
So all the positive charge and almost all the mass are packed in a tiny nucleus.
example.answer: Only the very few particles that came close to the tiny, dense, positive nucleus were pushed back.

learn.reallife: Scientists at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in Mumbai build on these atomic models when they work on nuclear energy and medicine.

games.title: Atomic models: true or false?
items: In Thomson's model, electrons are embedded in a sphere of positive charge
This is why it is compared to a watermelon with seeds, or a plum pudding.
Most alpha particles bounced back from the gold foil
Most passed straight through; only very few bounced back.
Rutherford concluded that most of the atom is empty space
Because most alpha particles went straight through without being deflected.
According to Bohr, electrons radiate energy while moving in their special orbits
Bohr said electrons in these orbits do not radiate energy, which keeps the atom stable.
It repelled the positive alpha particles that came close to it.

quiz.q: Who discovered the electron?
quiz.explain: J.J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 while studying cathode rays.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the discoverers of the electron and the neutron

quiz.q: Thomson's model of the atom is often compared to
quiz.explain: In Thomson's model, electrons sit in a positive sphere like seeds in the red part of a watermelon.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Thomson's model with the planet-like Rutherford model

quiz.q: In the gold foil experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the foil. What did this show?
options: Most of the atom is empty space
quiz.explain: If most particles meet nothing on their path, most of the space inside the atom must be empty.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the straight paths with empty space

quiz.q: Very few alpha particles bounced back from the gold foil. What did Rutherford conclude from this?
options: The atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus
The gold foil was too thick
The atom is negatively charged throughout
quiz.explain: Only a small, heavy, positively charged centre could push back a fast positive alpha particle, and it had to be tiny because so few hit it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks electrons caused the rebound, though they are far too light

quiz.q: Which particles did Rutherford fire at the gold foil?
quiz.explain: Rutherford used fast-moving, positively charged alpha particles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks electrons were fired, as in Thomson's experiments

quiz.q: What was the main drawback of Rutherford's model?
options: It could not explain why the atom is stable, since revolving electrons should lose energy and fall into the nucleus
quiz.explain: A charged particle moving in a circle should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus. Real atoms are stable, so the model needed improvement.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why a revolving electron would be a problem

quiz.q: What new idea did Bohr add to the model of the atom?
options: Electrons are embedded in positive charge
Electrons move only in certain fixed orbits without radiating energy
quiz.explain: Bohr proposed special orbits (shells) in which electrons do not lose energy. This explained why atoms are stable.
quiz.mistake: Credits Bohr with Thomson's or Chadwick's ideas

quiz.q: Why did Rutherford choose gold for his foil?
options: Gold can be beaten into extremely thin sheets
quiz.explain: Gold is very malleable, so a foil only about 1000 atoms thick could be made, letting alpha particles pass through.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gold was chosen for its value or colour

teach.ask: Gappu imagines the atom as a tiny solid marble: "Is an atom solid all the way through? How do we know what is inside?"
teach.praise: Chirp! Rutherford's gold foil experiment showed the atom is mostly empty space, with a tiny positive nucleus, and Bohr put the electrons in fixed shells around it!
teach.nudge: What did Rutherford see when he fired alpha particles at the gold foil? What did that tell him?

learn.hook: Carbon in your pencil and carbon used to date ancient wood are the same element, yet some of their atoms weigh more. How? Count the neutrons!
points: An atom has three main particles: the electron (charge −1, very small mass, about 1/1836 of a proton), the proton (charge +1, mass about 1 u) and the neutron (no charge, mass about 1 u). James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.
Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons move around it. In a neutral atom, number of electrons = number of protons.
Atomic number (Z) = number of protons. Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons. So neutrons = A − Z.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14, or chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

Isobars are atoms of different elements with the same mass number, such as calcium-40 (Z = 20) and argon-40 (Z = 18). Some isotopes are useful: uranium-235 is a nuclear fuel and cobalt-60 is used to treat cancer.

example.q: Think it through: Sodium has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. How many protons, electrons and neutrons does a neutral sodium atom have?

learn.reallife: Hospitals use radioactive isotopes for diagnosis and cancer treatment, and India's nuclear power plants use isotopes of uranium as fuel.

games.title: Match the particle or term
pairs: Same atomic number, different mass number

quiz.q: Who discovered the neutron?
quiz.explain: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.
quiz.mistake: Thinks Thomson, who found the electron, also found the neutron

quiz.q: The atomic number of an element is equal to the number of
quiz.explain: Atomic number Z is the number of protons in the nucleus. It decides which element the atom is.
quiz.mistake: Confuses atomic number with mass number

quiz.q: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. What is its mass number?
quiz.explain: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23.
quiz.mistake: Gives only the number of protons or of neutrons

quiz.q: Chlorine-35 has atomic number 17. How many neutrons does it have?
quiz.explain: Neutrons = A − Z = 35 − 17 = 18.
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of subtracting, or gives the atomic number

quiz.q: What are isotopes?
options: Atoms of different elements with the same mass number
Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers
quiz.explain: Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so their mass numbers differ.
quiz.mistake: Confuses isotopes with isobars

quiz.q: Which pair are isobars?
quiz.explain: Calcium-40 (Z = 20) and argon-40 (Z = 18) are different elements with the same mass number. The other pairs are isotopes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks isotopes and isobars mean the same thing

quiz.q: A neutral atom has 8 protons. How many electrons does it have?
quiz.explain: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the charges balance.
quiz.mistake: Thinks electrons equal the mass number or neutrons

quiz.q: What is the charge on a neutron?
quiz.explain: A neutron is neutral, as its name suggests. Protons are +1 and electrons are −1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every particle in the nucleus is positive

teach.ask: Gappu hears about carbon-12 and carbon-14: "If they have different numbers, how can they both be carbon?"
teach.praise: Tweet! Both have 6 protons, so both are carbon, but carbon-14 has 2 extra neutrons. Same atomic number, different mass number: isotopes!
teach.nudge: Which particle decides what element an atom is? And which particle is different in carbon-14?

learn.hook: Why is neon in glowing signboards so 'lazy' that it hardly reacts, while sodium reacts with water violently? It all depends on how electrons are arranged!
points: Electrons are arranged in shells K, L, M, N (n = 1, 2, 3, 4). The maximum number of electrons in a shell is 2n²: K = 2, L = 8, M = 18, N = 32.
Shells are filled step by step from the innermost one. For the first 18 elements, the outermost shell holds at most 8 electrons.
Examples: carbon (6) = 2, 4; oxygen (8) = 2, 6; sodium (11) = 2, 8, 1; chlorine (17) = 2, 8, 7; argon (18) = 2, 8, 8.
Electrons in the outermost shell are valence electrons. An outer shell with 8 electrons (an octet), or 2 for helium, is stable, so noble gases hardly react.

Valency is the combining capacity of an atom. If valence electrons are 1 to 4, valency = valence electrons; if 5 to 8, valency = 8 − valence electrons. Sodium has valency 1, oxygen 2, nitrogen 3 and carbon 4.

example.q: Think it through: Magnesium has atomic number 12. Write its electronic configuration and find its valency.
steps: K shell takes 2, L shell takes 8: that uses 10.
The remaining 2 go into the M shell: 2, 8, 2.
Two valence electrons, which it can lose to get an octet, so valency = 2.

learn.reallife: Electronic configuration explains why table salt forms from sodium and chlorine, and why helium is used in balloons safely: it does not react.

items.text: The K shell can hold at most ___ electrons.
An outer shell with 8 electrons is called an ___.
Noble gases such as neon have a valency of ___.

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of electrons the L shell (n = 2) can hold?
quiz.explain: Maximum electrons = 2n² = 2 × 2² = 8.
quiz.mistake: Uses 2n instead of 2n²

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of electrons the M shell (n = 3) can hold?
quiz.explain: Maximum electrons = 2n² = 2 × 3² = 18.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every shell holds only 8 electrons

quiz.q: What is the electronic configuration of sodium (atomic number 11)?
quiz.explain: Fill K with 2, L with 8, and the last electron goes into M: 2, 8, 1.
quiz.mistake: Puts more than 8 electrons in the L shell or fills the shells out of order

quiz.q: What is the electronic configuration of chlorine (atomic number 17)?
quiz.explain: K takes 2, L takes 8, and the remaining 7 go into M: 2, 8, 7.
quiz.mistake: Fills the shells in the wrong order

quiz.q: Magnesium has the configuration 2, 8, 2. What is its valency?
quiz.explain: Magnesium has 2 valence electrons, which it gives away to get an octet, so its valency is 2.
quiz.mistake: Uses the atomic number or 8 − 2 as the valency

quiz.q: Oxygen has the configuration 2, 6. What is its valency?
quiz.explain: Oxygen needs 2 more electrons to complete its octet, so valency = 8 − 6 = 2.
quiz.mistake: Takes the number of valence electrons (6) as the valency

quiz.q: Why does neon (2, 8) hardly react with other elements?
options: Its outermost shell is complete with 8 electrons
quiz.explain: Neon already has a stable octet in its outer shell, so it does not need to gain, lose or share electrons.
quiz.mistake: Does not link stability with a complete outer shell

quiz.q: Which element has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 3?
quiz.explain: 2 + 8 + 3 = 13 electrons, so the atomic number is 13, which is aluminium.
quiz.mistake: Looks only at the last number (3) and picks boron (2, 3)

teach.ask: Gappu counts on his feathers: "How do I know which shell each electron goes into? And why do some atoms react but others don't?"
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Fill K with 2, then L with 8, and so on. The outer electrons decide valency, and a full octet makes an atom stable and unreactive!
teach.nudge: How many electrons can the first shell take before we move on to the next one?
